Abstract 205

Endometriosis is a common condition associated with debilitating pelvic pain and infertility. 206

A genome-wide association study meta-analysis, including 60,674 cases and 701,926 207

controls of European and East Asian descent, identified 42 genome-wide significant loci 208

comprising 49 distinct association signals. Effect sizes were largest for stage III/IV disease, 209

driven by ovarian endometriosis. Identified signals explained up to 5.01% of disease 210

variance and regulated expression or methylation of genes in endometrium and blood, 211

many of which were associated with pain perception/maintenance (SRP14/BMF, GDAP1, 212

MLLT10, BSN, NGF). We observed significant genetic correlations between endometriosis 213

and 11 pain-conditions including migraine, back, and multisite chronic pain (MCP), as well as 214

inflammatory conditions including asthma and osteoarthritis. Multi-trait genetic analyses 215

identified substantial sharing of variants associated with endometriosis and MCP/migraine. 216

Targeted investigations of genetically regulated mechanisms shared between endometriosis 217

and other pain-conditions are needed to aid the development of new treatments and 218

facilitate early symptomatic intervention. 219

Endometriosis is an inflammatory condition occurring in 5-10% of women of reproductive 229

age associated with debilitating pelvic pain and infertility1. It is characterized by the 230

presence of endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus, mainly on pelvic organs. Definitive 231

diagnosis requires visualization of lesions during surgery, resulting in a delay in diagnosis 232

that globally averages 7 years from symptom onset2. Treatments are limited to surgical 233

removal of disease and adhesions, or hormonal treatments which can have problematic 234

side-effects. Endometriosis is a heterogeneous condition, typically classified according to 235

revised American Society of Reproductive Medicine (rASRM) criteria based on surgical 236

visualisation of disease. Stage I/II disease features superficial peritoneal lesions and minimal 237

adhesions, and stage III/IV more extensive disease including cystic ovarian endometriosis 238

(endometrioma), and extensive scarring, fibrosis and adhesions3. Presence of deep 239

endometriosis (lesions with >5mm depth that can infiltrate bowel, ureter, bladder, including 240

rectovaginal lesions) is not accounted for in the rASRM staging algorithm. 241

242

Causes of endometriosis remain largely unknown, but the condition has an estimated 243

heritability of ~ 50%4,5 with ~26% estimated due to common genetic variation6. Nine 244

genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of endometriosis in women of European and East 245

Asian ancestry have been reported to date7. The largest comprised 17,045 cases and 246

191,596 controls and identified 19 distinct associations at genome-wide significance 247

(p<5x10-8) mapping to 13 loci separated by >1Mb8, together explaining 1.75% of phenotypic 248

variance for endometriosis. Although positional evidence has suggested potential 249

involvement of sex-steroid hormone signalling, WNT signaling, cell adhesion/migration, cell 250

growth/carcinogenesis and inflammation-related pathways, the regulatory effects of most 251

of these loci in tissues relevant to endometriosis have yet to be determined. Moreover, the 252

causal variants driving the identified association signals and their functional involvement in 253

mediating the underlying pathogenic mechanisms are unknown. 254

255

Previous GWAS analyses have highlighted that effect sizes of most known risk-variants are 256

larger for rASRM stage III/IV disease3,8, but associations with specific phenotypic 257

characteristics in this broad classification (e.g. cystic ovarian endometriosis (endometrioma), 258

advanced scarring, fibrosis and adhesions) are unclear. Sub-phenotype analyses focused on 259

infertility, pain symptomatology, and surgical phenotypes beyond rASRM stage could help 260

decipher causal mechanisms contributing to various components of the complex underlying 261

pathophysiology and ultimately better targeted treatments. 262

263

Here, we report results elucidating the pathogenesis of endometriosis and its association 264

with sub-phenotypes derived from the largest GWAS meta-analysis of endometriosis to 265

date, including 60,674 cases and 701,926 controls of European and East Asian ancestry, 266

followed by fine-mapping of causal variants and comprehensive investigation of their 267

functional effects in endometrium, blood and other relevant tissues, as well as sub- 268

phenotype and comorbidity analyses. 269

Results 271

We conducted a meta-analysis of 24 GWAS with a total effective sample size of 206,106 272

(60,674 cases and 701,926 controls) of European (98%: Europe, USA, Australia), and East 273

Asian (2%: Japan) ancestry. In 12 GWAS, women had surgically confirmed endometriosis 274

including 3,916 with rASRM stage I/II and 4,045 with rASRM stage III/IV disease; in 9 studies, 275

3,060 cases had known infertility in addition to endometriosis (Supplementary Table 1). 276

Each GWAS dataset was imputed up to 1000 Genomes (1000G P3v5), Haplotype Reference 278

Consortium (HRC r1.1 2016) or population-specific whole genome sequence data, and 279

standardised quality control was performed (Methods; Supplementary Table 2). Meta- 280

analysis was conducted for 10,401,531 SNPs under a fixed-effects model with inverse- 281

variance weighting for overall, rASRM stage I/II, rASRM stage III/IV and endometriosis 282

associated infertility (Extended Data Fig. 1-2). 283

284

GWAS meta-analysis reveals 42 loci for endometriosis 285

We identified 42 genome-wide significant loci (p<5x10-8) for overall endometriosis, 31 of 286

which have not been previously reported (Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 3, Extended Data 287

Figs. 1-2); 12 of the 42 loci were significant at a more stringent p<5x10-9 threshold, 288

suggested as more appropriate for whole genome sequence data. Following earlier 289

observations of a greater genetic contribution to rASRM stage III/IV endometriosis9, we 290

conducted sub-phenotype analyses including rASRM stage III/IV (4,045 cases/379,890 291

controls), rASRM stage I/II (3,916 cases/184,006 controls) and endometriosis-associated 292

infertility (3,060 cases/242,555 controls). No additional genome-wide association signals 293

were detected in sub-phenotype analyses; of the 42 loci, eight reached genome-wide 294

significance for stage III/IV, one for endometriosis-associated infertility but none for stage 295

I/II. However, lead SNPs at 38/42 genome-wide significant loci showed larger effect sizes in 296

stage III/IV vs. stage I/II analysis, and of these, 6 with non-overlapping 95% confidence 297

intervals between the sub-phenotypes (KDR/4q12, SYNE1/6q25.1, 7p15.2/7p15.2, CDKN2- 298

BAS1/9p21.3, SLC19A2/1q24.2, IGF1/12q23.2) (Fig. 1; Supplementary Table 3; 299

Supplementary Figs. 1-2). 300

Sensitivity analyses to test the impact of small datasets and the inclusion of male controls in 305

7, Extended data Figs 1e and 3). 307

308

Multiple association signals at endometriosis risk loci 309

To identify the presence of multiple distinct associations at the 42 genome-wide significant 310

loci, we conducted approximate conditional analysis based on summary meta-analysis 311

results restricted to European ancestry GWAS. Four loci had multiple distinct associations 312

after conditioning (p<5x10-8; see Methods) including three with two signals (GREB1/2p25.1, 313

CDKN2-BAS1/ 9p21.3, IGF1/12q23.2); and SYNE1/6q25.1 with five signals (Supplementary 314

*Table 3). In total, 49 index SNPs representing distinct associations were identified across the 315*

42 endometriosis loci (Supplementary Table 8; Supplementary Fig. 6). 316

317

The phenotypic variance for overall endometriosis explained by the 42 lead SNPs was 1.62% 318

vs. 1.98% by the 49 index SNPs. Meta-analysis limited to datasets with surgically/medically 319

ascertained cases, less prone to misclassification bias and potentially including women with 320

more severe symptoms, showed that the 42 lead SNPs explained 3.99% of endometriosis 321

variance, and the 49 index SNPs 4.79%. For stage III/IV disease, the 42 lead SNPs explained 322

4.10% and 49 index SNPs 5.01% of disease variance (Supplementary Table 9). 323

Fine-mapping of endometriosis association signals 325

To identify potential causal variants, we performed fine-mapping based on the European 326

ancestry-specific meta-analysis results; 99% credible sets were constructed assuming a 327

single causal SNP driving each of the 49 distinct association signals (Supplementary Table 328

10-12; see Methods). For seven association signals, credible SNP sets containing ≤10 SNPs 329

were observed. Fine-mapping uncovered 6 “high-confidence” variants (posterior probability 330

(ʋ) >50% to be causal): rs71575922 in SYNE1 and rs73625113 in ESR1; rs6456259 in LNC- 331

LBCS; rs6970537 in HOXA10 and rs3803042 1kb downstream of HOXC10; and rs73241342 in 332

LINC00629 (Supplementary Table 13). All were in non-coding regions. 333

334

Genetic regulation of expression and methylation at endometriosis risk loci 335

Genes located within ±200kb of each of the 49 index SNPs were enriched for expression in 336

endometrium, smooth muscle (Human Protein Atlas) and uterus (GTex) (see Supplementary 337

text; Extended Data Figs. 4a-d). To identify specific genes regulated by the 49 distinct 338

endometriosis association signals, we analysed four expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) 339

datasets: 1) a gene expression microarray study of 229 endometrial samples10; 2) a meta- 340

analysis of RNAseq-based eQTL datasets including 368 endometrial samples (11 and 341

Supplementary Tables 34-35; see Methods); 3) RNAseq expression data from 129  uterus 342

tissue samples from GTEx; and 4) data from 31,684 blood samples from the eQTLGen 343

Consortium12. We also associated SNPs in the endometriosis risk regions with DNA 344

methylation of nearby CpG sites in endometrium and blood using previously published mQTL 345

datasets (Supplementary Table 17).13,14 346

Summary data-based Mendelian Randomisation (SMR)15 was used to identify genes whose 348

expression (eQTL) or methylation (mQTL) levels are associated with endometriosis due to the 349

effects of a common genetic variant (either by direct causal or pleiotropic effects) rather than 350

due to linkage disequilibrium (LD). Table 1 summarises the significant eQTL/mQTL SMR results 351

across endometriosis GWAS loci, together with evidence from chromatin interactions (see 352

Supplementary Text, Supplementary Tables 14-19, and Extended Data Figs 5-6 for detailed 353

results). 354

355

Observations that endometriosis risk variants on chromosomes 2p25.1 and 12q22 may 356

function through changes in expression/methylation of GREB1, and VEZT and/or FGD6, 357

respectively, have been reported previously10,11,16. Many of the other potentially causal genes 358

have strong biological support. Notable was the signal for GDAP1 (GDAP1/8q21.11), 359

previously associated with dysmenorrhea severity and neuronal development (Fig. 2)17,18. 360

Rs4567029 regulates methylation of probes near GDAP1 and is in perfect LD with rs10283076 361

that was identified as the variant regulating GDAP1 expression in blood tissue (Supplementary 362

*Table 16). The SRP14-AS1/15q15.1 locus harbored multiple distinct association signals in 363*

endometrium and blood and chromatin interaction with BMF (Bcl2 modifying factor) (Fig. 3; 364

Supplementary Tables 15,16,18). BMF encodes for a glycoprotein associated with sex 365

hormone binding globulin and regulating bioavailability of oestrogen and testosterone19. 366

Variants in SRP14 may also affect endometriosis-associated pain genesis and maintenance 367

through regulation of DHEA-sulfate (DHEA-S) levels20. DHEA-S is a neurosteroid functioning as 368

a neurotropin, that can bind and activate nerve growth factor (NGF) and brain-derived 369

neurotrophic factor (BDNF)21,22. BDNF has been shown to regulate the maintenance of chronic 370

pain in various chronic disorders23, and its expression appears increased in the eutopic 371

We next investigated whether the endometriosis-associated genes identified through SMR 376

analyses (Table 1) are expressed in specific cell types. We used the large GTEx single cell 377

expression database, although this was limited to cellular components from 8 tissues not 378

including endometrium, ovary or blood (see Methods). Of the 23 genes, 18 were expressed 379

in cells included in the GTEx single cell database, (Extended Data Fig. 7). BMF, GDAP1, 380

MLLT10, TRA2A, SRP14, SYNE1, and VEZT and were expressed in neuronal and 381

neuroendocrine cells. CALCRL, MLLT10, SYNE1, TRA2A, and VEZT were expressed in 382

adipocytes, endothelial cells and fibroblasts and a cluster of genes including ARL14EP, ESR1, 383

SYNE1, MLLT10, TRA2A and VEZT were expressed in immune cells, most commonly B cells 384

and T cells. Epithelial cells expressed ABO, ESR1, MLLT10, TRA2A, SRP14, SYNE1, and VEZT. 385

The SMR results from endometrium and blood implicated several causal genes associated 387

with mechanisms of pain perception and maintenance (SRP14/BMF, GDAP1, MLLT10, BSN, 388

NGF). We next investigated the association of the GWAS loci with sub-phenotypes of 389

Discussion 553

In this study we identified 42 loci with 49 distinct signals associated with endometriosis, a 3- 554

fold increase from previous studies8. Most had larger effect sizes for stage III/IV disease, and 555

combined they explained 5.01% of stage III/IV disease variance. Our sub-phenotype analysis 556

provided evidence that the presence of ovarian endometriosis drives the larger effect sizes 557

for stage III/IV disease at least in part, with a genetic basis that is distinct from other disease 558

manifestations. While we did not observe significant differences in effect sizes between 559

endometriosis and adenomyosis (sometimes referred to as “endometriosis of the uterus”)58, 560

the correlation of effects was highest with stage I/II endometriosis and superficial peritoneal 561


<!-- Page 23 -->


22

lesions suggesting a shared pathogenesis of these subtypes, or their associated symptoms, 562

with adenomyosis. Important caveats are the potential for misclassification of ICD-defined 563

adenomyosis as controls59 (although this will have applied similarly to endometriosis 564

diagnoses) and the modest sample size of adenomyosis-only cases. 565

566

The SMR analyses linking variants at the identified risk loci to expression and DNA 567

methylation differences in endometrium and blood identified numerous functional insights 568

into the mechanisms through which endometriosis association signals are mediated. 569

Potentially causal relationships were observed with genes expressed in endometrium 570

(SRP14, HOXB9, TRA2A, with previous evidence confirmed for VEZT/FGD9 and GREB1) 11,14,60 571

and in blood (including ABO, ESR1/SYNE1, GDAP1, FSHB, MLLT10, SRP14-AS1, WNT4). Many 572

of these genes are expressed in different cell types relevant to endometriosis pathogenesis, 573

including neuronal cells, immune cells, and epithelial cells; eQTL studies associating genetic 574

variants to cell-specific expression patterns in endometrium and peritoneal fluid are needed 575

to dissect differential regulation at a cellular level. 576

577

The genes causally related to endometriosis risk variants have functions in sex-hormone 578

driven signalling, uterine development, oncogenesis, inflammatory adhesion molecules and 579

angiogenic factors. Particularly notable, however, was the link of many of the genes 580

identified, such as SRP14/BMF, GDAP1, MLLT10, BSN, NGF, as well as ‘hormone regulators’ 581

SYNE1/ESR1 and FSHB, to mechanisms of pain perception and maintenance.  Our genetic 582

correlation analysis highlighted significant correlations between endometriosis and 11 pain 583

conditions - including migraine, headache, dorsalgia, chronic back pain and MCP. Multi-trait 584

analysis of GWAS summary statistics between endometriosis, MCP and migraine, 585


<!-- Page 24 -->


23

highlighted many additional genome-wide significant variants, 12 mapping within 500Kb 586

across diseases and 9 tagging the same association signals. These results provide support to 587

the hypothesis that the presence of endometriosis can result in pain through interlinked 588

activation of hormonal, immune, and neuronal pathways as is seen in other chronic pain 589

conditions61. It also provides strong support for further investigation of the mechanisms 590

underlying the genetically regulated comorbidity between endometriosis and other types of 591

pain, both to aid the development of new treatments that facilitate early intervention and 592

rationalise the repurposing of currently available therapies. 593

594

We also observed significant genetic correlations between endometriosis and two 595

inflammatory conditions: asthma and osteoarthritis. Asthma has previously been associated 596

with endometriosis in epidemiological studies62,63, and a shared genetic target with was 597

recently highlighted64. Endometriosis has also previously been linked epidemiologically to 598

increased risk of joint inflammation, but mainly in relation to rheumatoid arthritis, an auto- 599

immune condition65, and not osteoarthritis characterised by auto-inflammation66. This link 600

has not been fully explored as the onset of osteoarthritis would typically post-date an 601

endometriosis diagnosis by several decades, and many musculoskeletal cohorts do not 602

capture detailed women’s health data.  Given that osteoarthritis also appears to be 603

associated with fluctuations in sex hormones67 a more detailed exploration into the 604

genetically driven shared pathogenesis of these conditions is warranted. 605

606

Our results demonstrate genetic underpinning of shared pathogenesis of endometriosis 607

with other chronic pain conditions, as well as other inflammatory conditions. Our 608

identification of a range of genes with strong evidence for causal association with 609


<!-- Page 25 -->


24

endometriosis, should inform new avenues of targeted research into gene-specific 610

mechanisms of pain and pathogenesis, with the potential to identify new - or repurposing of 611

existing - treatment targets for this debilitating, enigmatic disease. 612

Abstract 205

Endometriosis is a common condition associated with debilitating pelvic pain and infertility. 206

A genome-wide association study meta-analysis, including 60,674 cases and 701,926 207

controls of European and East Asian descent, identified 42 genome-wide significant loci 208

comprising 49 distinct association signals. Effect sizes were largest for stage III/IV disease, 209

driven by ovarian endometriosis. Identified signals explained up to 5.01% of disease 210

variance and regulated expression or methylation of genes in endometrium and blood, 211

many of which were associated with pain perception/maintenance (SRP14/BMF, GDAP1, 212

MLLT10, BSN, NGF). We observed significant genetic correlations between endometriosis 213

and 11 pain-conditions including migraine, back, and multisite chronic pain (MCP), as well as 214

inflammatory conditions including asthma and osteoarthritis. Multi-trait genetic analyses 215

identified substantial sharing of variants associated with endometriosis and MCP/migraine. 216

Targeted investigations of genetically regulated mechanisms shared between endometriosis 217

and other pain-conditions are needed to aid the development of new treatments and 218

facilitate early symptomatic intervention. 219

Endometriosis is an inflammatory condition occurring in 5-10% of women of reproductive 229

age associated with debilitating pelvic pain and infertility1. It is characterized by the 230

presence of endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus, mainly on pelvic organs. Definitive 231

diagnosis requires visualization of lesions during surgery, resulting in a delay in diagnosis 232

that globally averages 7 years from symptom onset2. Treatments are limited to surgical 233

removal of disease and adhesions, or hormonal treatments which can have problematic 234

side-effects. Endometriosis is a heterogeneous condition, typically classified according to 235

revised American Society of Reproductive Medicine (rASRM) criteria based on surgical 236

visualisation of disease. Stage I/II disease features superficial peritoneal lesions and minimal 237

adhesions, and stage III/IV more extensive disease including cystic ovarian endometriosis 238

(endometrioma), and extensive scarring, fibrosis and adhesions3. Presence of deep 239

endometriosis (lesions with >5mm depth that can infiltrate bowel, ureter, bladder, including 240

rectovaginal lesions) is not accounted for in the rASRM staging algorithm. 241

242

Causes of endometriosis remain largely unknown, but the condition has an estimated 243

heritability of ~ 50%4,5 with ~26% estimated due to common genetic variation6. Nine 244

genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of endometriosis in women of European and East 245

Asian ancestry have been reported to date7. The largest comprised 17,045 cases and 246

191,596 controls and identified 19 distinct associations at genome-wide significance 247

(p<5x10-8) mapping to 13 loci separated by >1Mb8, together explaining 1.75% of phenotypic 248

variance for endometriosis. Although positional evidence has suggested potential 249

involvement of sex-steroid hormone signalling, WNT signaling, cell adhesion/migration, cell 250

growth/carcinogenesis and inflammation-related pathways, the regulatory effects of most 251

of these loci in tissues relevant to endometriosis have yet to be determined. Moreover, the 252


<!-- Page 64 -->


9

causal variants driving the identified association signals and their functional involvement in 253

mediating the underlying pathogenic mechanisms are unknown. 254

255

Previous GWAS analyses have highlighted that effect sizes of most known risk-variants are 256

larger for rASRM stage III/IV disease3,8, but associations with specific phenotypic 257

characteristics in this broad classification (e.g. cystic ovarian endometriosis (endometrioma), 258

advanced scarring, fibrosis and adhesions) are unclear. Sub-phenotype analyses focused on 259

infertility, pain symptomatology, and surgical phenotypes beyond rASRM stage could help 260

decipher causal mechanisms contributing to various components of the complex underlying 261

pathophysiology and ultimately better targeted treatments. 262

263

Here, we report results elucidating the pathogenesis of endometriosis and its association 264

with sub-phenotypes derived from the largest GWAS meta-analysis of endometriosis to 265

date, including 60,674 cases and 701,926 controls of European and East Asian ancestry, 266

followed by fine-mapping of causal variants and comprehensive investigation of their 267

functional effects in endometrium, blood and other relevant tissues, as well as sub- 268

phenotype and comorbidity analyses. 269

We conducted a meta-analysis of 24 GWAS with a total effective sample size of 206,106 272

(60,674 cases and 701,926 controls) of European (98%: Europe, USA, Australia), and East 273

Asian (2%: Japan) ancestry. In 12 GWAS, women had surgically confirmed endometriosis 274

including 3,916 with rASRM stage I/II and 4,045 with rASRM stage III/IV disease; in 9 studies, 275

3,060 cases had known infertility in addition to endometriosis (Supplementary Table 1). 276

We identified 42 genome-wide significant loci (p<5x10-8) for overall endometriosis, 31 of 286

Discussion 553

In this study we identified 42 loci with 49 distinct signals associated with endometriosis, a 3- 554

fold increase from previous studies8. Most had larger effect sizes for stage III/IV disease, and 555

combined they explained 5.01% of stage III/IV disease variance. Our sub-phenotype analysis 556

provided evidence that the presence of ovarian endometriosis drives the larger effect sizes 557

for stage III/IV disease at least in part, with a genetic basis that is distinct from other disease 558

manifestations. While we did not observe significant differences in effect sizes between 559

endometriosis and adenomyosis (sometimes referred to as “endometriosis of the uterus”)58, 560

the correlation of effects was highest with stage I/II endometriosis and superficial peritoneal 561


<!-- Page 77 -->


22

lesions suggesting a shared pathogenesis of these subtypes, or their associated symptoms, 562

with adenomyosis. Important caveats are the potential for misclassification of ICD-defined 563

adenomyosis as controls59 (although this will have applied similarly to endometriosis 564

diagnoses) and the modest sample size of adenomyosis-only cases. 565

566

The SMR analyses linking variants at the identified risk loci to expression and DNA 567

methylation differences in endometrium and blood identified numerous functional insights 568

into the mechanisms through which endometriosis association signals are mediated. 569

Potentially causal relationships were observed with genes expressed in endometrium 570

(SRP14, HOXB9, TRA2A, with previous evidence confirmed for VEZT/FGD9 and GREB1) 11,14,60 571

and in blood (including ABO, ESR1/SYNE1, GDAP1, FSHB, MLLT10, SRP14-AS1, WNT4). Many 572

of these genes are expressed in different cell types relevant to endometriosis pathogenesis, 573

including neuronal cells, immune cells, and epithelial cells; eQTL studies associating genetic 574

variants to cell-specific expression patterns in endometrium and peritoneal fluid are needed 575

to dissect differential regulation at a cellular level. 576

577

The genes causally related to endometriosis risk variants have functions in sex-hormone 578

driven signalling, uterine development, oncogenesis, inflammatory adhesion molecules and 579

angiogenic factors. Particularly notable, however, was the link of many of the genes 580

identified, such as SRP14/BMF, GDAP1, MLLT10, BSN, NGF, as well as ‘hormone regulators’ 581

SYNE1/ESR1 and FSHB, to mechanisms of pain perception and maintenance.  Our genetic 582

correlation analysis highlighted significant correlations between endometriosis and 11 pain 583

conditions - including migraine, headache, dorsalgia, chronic back pain and MCP. Multi-trait 584

analysis of GWAS summary statistics between endometriosis, MCP and migraine, 585


<!-- Page 78 -->


23

highlighted many additional genome-wide significant variants, 12 mapping within 500Kb 586

across diseases and 9 tagging the same association signals. These results provide support to 587

the hypothesis that the presence of endometriosis can result in pain through interlinked 588

activation of hormonal, immune, and neuronal pathways as is seen in other chronic pain 589

conditions61. It also provides strong support for further investigation of the mechanisms 590

underlying the genetically regulated comorbidity between endometriosis and other types of 591

pain, both to aid the development of new treatments that facilitate early intervention and 592

rationalise the repurposing of currently available therapies. 593

594

We also observed significant genetic correlations between endometriosis and two 595

inflammatory conditions: asthma and osteoarthritis. Asthma has previously been associated 596

with endometriosis in epidemiological studies62,63, and a shared genetic target with was 597

recently highlighted64. Endometriosis has also previously been linked epidemiologically to 598

increased risk of joint inflammation, but mainly in relation to rheumatoid arthritis, an auto- 599

immune condition65, and not osteoarthritis characterised by auto-inflammation66. This link 600

has not been fully explored as the onset of osteoarthritis would typically post-date an 601

endometriosis diagnosis by several decades, and many musculoskeletal cohorts do not 602

capture detailed women’s health data.  Given that osteoarthritis also appears to be 603

associated with fluctuations in sex hormones67 a more detailed exploration into the 604

genetically driven shared pathogenesis of these conditions is warranted. 605

606

Our results demonstrate genetic underpinning of shared pathogenesis of endometriosis 607

with other chronic pain conditions, as well as other inflammatory conditions. Our 608

identification of a range of genes with strong evidence for causal association with 609

Multi-trait analysis of GWASs. MTAG is a generalisation of standard inverse-variance 1292

weighted meta-analysis framework. It takes pre-processed GWAS summary statistics from 1293
